summary: Sitting opposite the temple treasury, Jesus watches a poor widow drop in two tiny coins and tells His disciples she has given more than all the rich.
key_insight: Jesus does not say she gave more than any one of the rich. He says she put in “more than all those who have given to the treasury,” more than all of them together. He measures a gift by what the giver has left: they gave from abundance; she gave everything.
story: Jesus sat down opposite the temple treasury and watched how the people put in their money. Many who were rich put in much. {Mk}
Then a poor widow came and threw in two mites, which make a quadrans. {Mk}
Jesus called His disciples to Himself {Mk} and said, “Assuredly, I say to you that this poor widow has put in more than all those who have given to the treasury.” {Mk}
The others had given offerings for God out of their abundance. {Lk} She had given out of her poverty: “all that she had, her whole livelihood.” {Mk}
differences: Mark alone says Jesus sat opposite the treasury and called His disciples to Himself; Luke says He looked up and saw the rich putting in their gifts.
Mark explains the coins for his readers: two mites “make a quadrans,” a Roman coin. Luke mentions only the two mites.
Mark says she gave “all that she had, her whole livelihood”; Luke says “all the livelihood that she had,” and adds that the rich gave “offerings for God.”

scene.label: The treasury
scene.text: The treasury was in the Court of the Women, a court open to all Israelites, men and women alike. Later Jewish writings describe thirteen trumpet-shaped chests there, each marked for a different offering. From where Jesus sat, the giving was in plain view.

scene.label: Two mites
scene.text: The mite (Greek lepton) was the smallest copper coin in use in Judea. Two made a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin, worth one sixty-fourth of a denarius, a laborer’s daily wage. She could have kept one coin back.

scene.label: Widows in Israel
scene.text: With no husband and often no son to provide for her, a widow was among the most exposed people in the land. The Law told Israel to leave part of every harvest for her (Deuteronomy 24:19–21), and the prophets condemned leaders who made widows “their prey” (Isaiah 10:2).

witnesses.mark: Explains the coins in Roman terms, a sign he wrote with Roman readers in mind, and shows Jesus calling His disciples over to make sure they saw. Mark sets the widow right after the warning about scribes who “devour widows’ houses” (12:40) and right before Jesus foretells the temple’s fall (13:1–2).
witnesses.luke: Tells the story in a few lines and keeps it within his steady attention to wealth and the poor (6:20, 24; 12:15–21; 16:19–31). Right after it, others admire the temple “adorned with beautiful stones and donations” (21:5); Jesus had just shown them the donation that mattered most.

seeing.reveals: Jesus sees what no one else in the court noticed. He weighs gifts by their cost and the heart behind them, not their size, and He calls His disciples to look where He is looking.
seeing.living: Jesus did not call her foolish or tell her to keep something back; He honored her. Give to God in a way that truly costs you, and stop measuring gifts, yours or anyone else’s, by their size. The One who watched the treasury that day still counts what is given by what is left behind.
seeing.ponder: What would it look like for you to trust God with something you cannot afford to lose?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus measures a gift not by what is given, but by what is left.
outline: A gift too small to notice (42)
preaching.watch_for: Read verses 38–44 together. The scribes “devour widows’ houses” (12:40); a widow gives “her whole livelihood” (12:44). Some read the scene as Jesus lamenting a system that took a widow’s last coins, but His own words commend her gift.
